May Byron's 1915 Yorkshire parkin, made dairy-free

Rub the lard and butter into the flour, add all dry ingredients, warm the treacle, and add with a little milk, mix well, pour into a flat tin, well greased. Bake in a very moderate oven about forty minutes.
May Byron, Pot-Luck or The British Home Cookery Book, 1915
About 20 minutes, plus at least a few days resting
20 cm (8-inch) square tin, at least 4 cm deep
ground oats, not porridge oats: see notes
other blocks or lard: see Making it dairy-free
1 tsp; buy at the supermarket or
a pinch; omit if using a salted baking block
Preheat the oven to 150°C (300°F). Line a 20 cm (8-inch) square tin.
Warm the golden syrup, black treacle and water gently in a saucepan, stirring, until runny and mixed. Don't let it boil.
Mix the flour and oatmeal. Rub in the fat, lifting the mixture and letting it fall back into the bowl to add air.
Stir in the sugar, ginger, mixed spice, baking powder and salt. Mix thoroughly.
Mix in the warm syrup. The batter should be thick but pourable; add a little more water only if it's too stiff.
Pour into the tin, smooth the top and bake for 45 minutes.
Cool in the tin for 10 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack to cool completely.
Leave it at least a few days, ideally a week, before eating. It starts out dry and becomes soft and sticky. Cut into 16 squares to serve.

The original recipe's 55 g lard, 55 g butter and 60 ml milk bring about 101.7 g of fat and 63.2 g of water to the batter. The swap keeps both totals: the fat becomes a dairy-free block, lard or a mix, and the milk becomes water. The main recipe uses a 75% block and no lard.
L = the share of the fat you want as lard, from 0 (none) to 100 (all)
P = the block's fat %, from its label (75 in the main recipe)
W = the block's water %, if you know it; if not, use 98 − P
Use a block, not a tub spread: tubs are softer and wetter, so they smear instead of rubbing in to crumbs.

The formula assumes butter is 81% fat and 16% water and whole milk is 3.5% fat and 88% water. Labels rarely give a block's water, so 98 − P assumes about 2% of it is neither fat nor water (salt and emulsifier). These are typical values, so the batter has the final say: thick but pourable.
Use medium or fine oatmeal (ground oats, sometimes sold as "Scottish oatmeal"), not porridge oats. To make your own, pulse porridge oats in a food processor until they look like coarse sand.
